groups.instructions: Read the article about mapping neighborhood sounds and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A Map Made of Everyday Sounds

When students in a geography class were asked to map their neighborhood, most expected to mark roads, shops, and parks. Their teacher proposed a different layer: sound. For one week, small groups visited the same public places at three times of day. At each stop, they spent two minutes listening before writing notes. They did not record private conversations or attempt to measure exact decibel levels. Instead, they classified sounds into broad categories such as traffic, voices, birds, machinery, and music.

The resulting maps showed that a place could change character without changing its physical layout. A square near the market was dominated by delivery vehicles early in the morning, by conversation at lunchtime, and by music from a nearby exercise class in the evening. A narrow lane that seemed quiet at noon became noisy when school ended. The students began to see time as part of a map rather than simply as a label beside it.

The exercise also revealed disagreement. Two students sometimes classified the same sound differently. Rather than treating this as a mistake to erase, the class discussed why categories can depend on attention and purpose. A cyclist might notice engines because they affect safety, while a shop owner might focus on voices because they signal customer activity.

The teacher concluded that the map was useful precisely because it was incomplete. It encouraged students to ask what conventional maps leave out and whose experience a map represents. The project did not replace ordinary maps. It added another way to notice how public space is used.

groups.instructions: Read the article about outdoor lighting and insect activity and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
When Night Becomes Too Bright

Street lighting makes evening travel safer and allows public spaces to remain usable after sunset. Yet outdoor light also changes the environment in ways that are easy to overlook. Insects, for example, often use natural light sources such as the moon to orient themselves. A bright artificial lamp can become a much stronger signal at close range, drawing some insects away from feeding or breeding areas.

Early discussions of this problem sometimes focused on the simple idea that “less light is better.” Researchers and city planners now tend to ask more specific questions. Where is light needed? At what time? In which direction should it shine? A lamp that sends most of its light downward onto a path may serve people better while disturbing fewer organisms than a brighter lamp that spills light into trees and windows. Timing also matters. A sports area may need strong lighting during an evening match but not at three in the morning.

Color is another factor. Different wavelengths affect species in different ways, and there is no single color that is harmless to every organism. This makes universal rules difficult. Still, experiments can compare alternatives under local conditions. A town might test two lamp designs on similar streets and observe visibility, energy use, insect activity, and resident feedback over several months.

Such trials require care because many things change at once. Weather influences insect numbers, trees grow leaves or lose them, and human activity varies with seasons. If a town changes lighting in only one location and observes it for one week, it may mistake a temporary pattern for a lasting effect. Longer comparisons and matched locations provide stronger evidence.

The broader lesson is that good lighting is a design problem rather than a contest between darkness and brightness. People need visibility, and ecosystems need periods of darkness. Thoughtful design seeks a workable balance by putting the right amount of light in the right place at the right time.
